lr-flaw-interface-tested-engineers: C is best (sample differs from population in a relevant respect), but B (employees reluctant to criticize own company's product) is a second defensible flaw since the stimulus relies partly on self-reported 'intuitive' descriptions. The objective task-completion data makes B weaker, but a strong test-taker could hesitate. Consider tightening B or removing the self-report element.
lr-flaw-insomnia-stress-sufficient-cause: A is best (capable-of-causing treated as did-cause), but C (undiagnosed physical illness) is also a legitimate vulnerability given the stimulus says only 'no diagnosed physical illness'. Both attack the same inference; A is more general. Mild two-answer risk.
lr-flaw-long-lived-firms-debt: E chosen (no consideration of low-borrowing firms that failed / survivor-only sample). D (reverse causation) is weakened by 'throughout its history' but some solvers may still pick it. Acceptable but note the pull.
lr-flaw-impartial-observer-tax-unjust: E (begging the question) chosen. A (ad hominem) is a plausible secondary read since the argument dismisses defenders as partial; the circular structure is the deeper flaw. Moderate two-answer risk.
lr-flaw-letters-editor-stadium: B chosen (self-selected letter writers). D (same few individuals wrote many letters) is a weaker but defensible alternative. Low risk.
lr-weaken-bike-lanes-cyclist-safety: E chosen (alternative cause: low speed limits). A (more cyclists) could be read as a safety-in-numbers alternative cause, though the per-kilometer metric blunts it. Low-moderate risk.
lr-necessary-assumption-aldric-eclipse-c: E is the targeted gap (chronicle eclipse must be one visible in the kingdom), but B (astronomical calculations reliable for the 9th century) is also defensible under the negation test since the argument leans entirely on that premise. Consider softening B (e.g., make it about a different century or overly broad) so only E survives.
lr-weaken-training-turnover-reverse: D (reverse causation) is best, but A also weakens by cutting the causal story; A is in tension with the stated correlation, which is why it loses, but it is a strong second. Acceptable as-is; flagging only because two choices weaken.
lr-must-be-true-ashgrove-library-vote: B is correct; D is a strong distractor that only fails because 'adopted only if five votes' is a necessary, not sufficient, condition. Intentional and fair, but expect pushback from test-takers who read 'only if' loosely.
lr-necessary-assumption-knee-surgery-ana: Minor: (B) 'reports were honest' is a soft second candidate under negation (dishonest reports would also undercut the evidence). (D) is clearly the intended alternate-cause gap and is the better answer, but (B) is closer to defensible than a typical distractor; consider making (B) more obviously wrong (e.g., 'perfectly accurate in every case').
lr-necessary-assumption-sarn-basin-ridge: Minor: (D) 'glacial movement never occurs without leaving deposits' is nearly a restatement of the stated premise 'Glaciers leave behind deposits,' so it reads as premise-restated rather than a clear wrong answer. (A) is the genuine gap (not found -> never present) and is the best answer; no change strictly required.
lr-necessary-assumption-export-firms-wag: Minor: (B) and (D) are plausible-looking because the stimulus mixes a correlation with a causal mechanism; (E) is the only one that survives negation cleanly. Acceptable as a hard item, but note that the two-part evidence structure makes (D) feel more tempting than usual.
lr-sufficient-assumption-ridgeline-docum: Minor: (E) (survey reliability) is a strong-looking competitor because the stimulus relies on survey data. (C) is the correct formal bridge (most viewers -> audience); (E) does not close that gap. Item is sound but (E) will draw many wrong answers.
lr-resolve-explain-payment-task-enjoymen: B is clearly best (dissonance-reduction mechanism explains the low-pay group's elevated rating), but E is a close distractor: it supplies a self-perception account for the high-pay group that a test-taker could read as also explaining the gap. E only addresses attribution of participation, not the enjoyment rating itself, so B wins, but the two choices sit closer than a typical credited/incorrect pair.
lr-resolve-explain-bicycle-gear-supplier: A is the answer. B (supplier farther away, in a neighboring country) is a plausible shipping/tariff explanation if 'spending on gears' is read to include delivered cost; it is weaker because it requires that assumption, but reviewers may want B tightened so it does not imply a cost increase.
lr-main-conclusion-kelver-flint-tools: D (final sentence, 'need not have had any contact') is the stated conclusion; B ('was not a southern outpost') overstates it. Defensible single answer, but the item hinges on a modal-strength distinction, so confirm the key is D and not B.
lr-argument-part-sentencing-guidelines: B chosen on 'Whatever the merits of that complaint' (explicit no-stand). But the closing clause 'a greater injustice than any the guidelines create' reads to some as conceding the guidelines do create injustice, which makes E a defensible trap. Consider tightening the stimulus so the judge's neutrality on the complaint is unambiguous (or, if E is intended, drop the 'whatever the merits' hedge).
lr-parallel-flaw-council-business-associ: E chosen (most A are B, most A are C, so most C are B, with C extending beyond A). D has the same surface form (most farms grow wheat / most farms family-owned -> most family-owned farms grow wheat) and is also invalid, differing only in the 'it is likely' hedge and in C being a subset of A. Two choices with the same flaw structure is risky; recommend rewriting D so its flaw is clearly different.
lr-method-of-reasoning-model-calibration: D chosen as the precise description of the dilemma structure ('Either way, her objection fails'). C (accusing the colleague of a double standard) is a strong second since the argument plainly implies it; acceptable as a trap, but note the two are close.
